symptoms: Vibrant green leaves without discoloration, lesions, or wilting
Normal vegetative and reproductive growth appropriate for plant age
Intact leaf sheaths and sturdy erect tillers
prevention: Maintain standard balanced nutrient management (NPK based on soil test)
Practice alternate wetting and drying (AWD) water management
Regular field monitoring and routine crop scouting
management: Continue routine cultural care and balanced fertilizer scheduling
organic_management: Maintain soil organic health and beneficial microbial biodiversity through compost and green manuring
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays healthy vegetative growth traits.
diseases.source: Standard Agronomic Field Guidelines (IRRI / ICAR Rice Knowledge Bank)

symptoms: Vibrant green leaves without discoloration, lesions, or wilting
Normal vegetative and reproductive growth appropriate for plant age
prevention: Maintain standard balanced nutrient management (NPK)
Practice recommended water management and regular field monitoring
management: Continue routine cultural care and periodic pest/disease scouting
organic_management: Maintain soil organic health and beneficial microbial biodiversity
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays healthy growth traits.
diseases.source: Standard Agronomic Field Guidelines (IRRI / ICAR Rice Knowledge Bank)

symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaf margins turning yellowish to grayish-white
Wavy margins along lesion borders with milky or amber bacterial ooze visible in high morning humidity
Severe early-stage infection causes seedling wilt and rolling known as 'kresek'
possible_causes: Pathogen transmission via irrigation water, rain splash, typhoons, and handling
Excessive nitrogen application and warm, humid weather (25-34°C with relative humidity >70%)
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant or tolerant cultivars (e.g. Improved Samba Mahsuri, IR64)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization; apply split doses with adequate potassium (potash)
Ensure proper field drainage and avoid flood water flow from infected fields into healthy fields
Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplanting
management: Drain field water intermittently to reduce canopy humidity
Delay or reduce subsequent top-dressed nitrogen applications until disease arrest
Eradicate weed hosts (such as Leersia oryzoides) along field bunds
organic_management: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg seed) or Bacillus subtilis
Foliar spray of 20% fresh cow dung extract or neem cake extract (5%)
Spray Panchagavya (3%) at 10-14 day intervals during vegetative growth
chemical_management: Copper hydroxide (2 g/L) or copper oxychloride (2.5 g/L) combined with Streptomycin sulfate + Tetracycline hydrochloride (300 ppm) where authorized by local extension guidelines
diseases.severity_notes: Can cause 20% to 50% yield loss if kresek or high flag leaf blighting occurs during early tillering and panicle emergence.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR-CRRI Rice Advisory Guidelines

symptoms: Narrow, water-soaked, translucent interveinal streaks running parallel to leaf veins
Streaks turn yellowish-brown to dark brown and are dotted with tiny amber-colored resinous droplets
Extensive lesions coalesce causing the entire leaf blade to turn brown, die, and shred in high winds
possible_causes: Bacterial entry through natural leaf stomata or mechanical wounds caused by wind and farm tools
Warm temperatures (28-32°C) combined with high relative humidity and stormy rainfall
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds from healthy seed plots
Adopt balanced nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium nutrition (avoid high nitrogen doses)
Maintain clean bunds and eliminate volunteer grass hosts
management: Avoid field operations while foliage is wet to prevent mechanical transmission
Practice alternate wetting and drying to reduce prolonged microclimatic moisture
organic_management: Seed treatment with bio-agents like Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma asperellum
Foliar spray with neem oil (3%) or botanicals (Vitex negundo leaf extract)
chemical_management: Foliar spray of Copper oxychloride (2.5 g/L) or Copper hydroxide (2.0 g/L) at early streak manifestation as per local extension protocols
diseases.severity_notes: Usually less destructive than bacterial leaf blight, but can cause 10-30% yield reduction under severe windstorm and high-moisture conditions.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & TNAU Agritech Portal

symptoms: Spikelets on emerging panicles turn pale green-yellow then reddish-brown
Infected grains remain blank and sterile, causing panicles to remain erect instead of drooping with grain weight
Panicle branches and rachis may turn dark brown, with infected seedlings exhibiting basal rot
possible_causes: Seed-borne inoculum flourishing under abnormally high nighttime temperatures (>22-25°C) during heading
Frequent rains and high relative humidity during flowering and grain fill
prevention: Plant certified pathogen-free, inspected seed stocks
Select planting dates to avoid heading during peak hot summer periods
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizers which delay maturity and increase floret susceptibility
management: Avoid sprinkler/overhead irrigation during flowering stage
Ensure field sanitation and deep plowing of crop residues post-harvest
organic_management: Seed soaking in bio-priming solutions with antagonistic Bacillus or Pseudomonas strains
Foliar bio-agent application before boot leaf emergence
chemical_management: Seed disinfection with designated bactericides (where registered); foliar options remain limited, focusing management on preventative cultural control and tolerant varieties
diseases.severity_notes: Highly destructive disease capable of causing up to 40-75% yield loss in susceptible varieties during unusually hot, humid flowering seasons.
diseases.source: FAO Plant Protection & LSU AgCenter Rice Pathology Guide

symptoms: Diamond-shaped or elliptical spindle lesions with whitish or grayish centers and brown/red borders on leaves
Dark necrotic ring lesions at the neck node directly below the panicle ('neck blast'), causing lodging and empty panicles ('whiteheads')
Rapid coalescing of leaf spots causing leaf death and burnt crop appearance
possible_causes: Airborne fungal conidia carried by wind and dew
High relative humidity (>90%), cool night temperatures (17-23°C), extended leaf wetness, and excessive nitrogen
prevention: Cultivate blast-resistant rice cultivars adapted to the region
Avoid dense seedling stands; optimize plant spacing to ensure air circulation
Apply nitrogen in 3 to 4 split applications rather than large single basal doses
Perform dry seed treatment with bio-agents or protectant fungicides
management: Maintain water layer in the field to inhibit spore germination (avoid prolonged dry soil stress)
Rogue infected volunteer plants and wild rice hosts from surrounding borders
organic_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride / harzianum (10 g/kg seed) or Pseudomonas fluorescens
Foliar spray of 5% neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) or fermented butter-milk (chaas) solution
Foliar application of bio-formulations like Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
chemical_management: Tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/L), Isoprothiolane 40% EC (1.5 mL/L), or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC (1 mL/L) applied at boot leaf and panicle emergence stages as per regional IPM recommendations
diseases.severity_notes: One of the most widespread and damaging rice diseases globally; neck blast phase can cause total yield failure.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR-NRRI Blast Advisory

symptoms: Diamond-shaped or spindle-shaped lesions with gray or whitish centers and brownish borders
Rapid expansion into large necrotic patches during periods of high dew and overcast weather
possible_causes: Fungal spores spreading through wind and morning dew
High relative humidity (>90%), cool nights, and high nitrogen rates
prevention: Plant blast-resistant varieties suited for the local agro-climatic zone
Avoid late planting and excessively dense seedling populations
management: Maintain continuous shallow flooding to reduce spore penetration
Avoid late-season top dressing with excessive nitrogen
organic_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride (10 g/kg)
Foliar spray with Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%)
chemical_management: Tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/L) or Kasugamycin 3% SL (2 mL/L) at first symptom appearance
diseases.severity_notes: Highly destructive under conducive weather; can cause complete leaf necrosis and significant vegetative yield reduction.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR Guidelines

symptoms: Dark grayish-brown lesions at the neck node directly below the panicle
Panicle branch breakage and incomplete grain filling resulting in white, empty heads ('whiteheads')
possible_causes: Severe leaf blast transition or late-season infection during panicle emergence
Continuous rainfall or morning fogs during the flowering to milky grain stage
prevention: Monitor leaf blast incidence closely prior to heading stage
Avoid water stress and high single-dose nitrogen at reproductive stages
management: Ensure timely preventative intervention prior to 50% heading in endemic areas
organic_management: Preventative bio-fungicide foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens at boot leaf stage
chemical_management: Tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/L) or Isoprothiolane 40% EC (1.5 mL/L) applied at boot leaf and repeat at 5% panicle emergence
diseases.severity_notes: Directly attacks the vascular collar supporting the panicle; can cause 50% to 100% loss of affected tillers.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR Guidelines

symptoms: Small, circular to oval dark brown spots on foliage with yellow halos
Older lesions show gray or whitish centers with prominent dark brown margins
Lesions coalesce causing leaf drying, dark spotting on glumes, and discolored 'pecky' grain
possible_causes: Airborne fungal conidia flourishing in nutrient-depleted or moisture-stressed soils
Soil deficiencies (especially potassium, silicon, manganese, and zinc)
Infected seed stocks and drought stress
prevention: Correct soil nutrient deficiencies based on regular soil health tests; ensure adequate potash (K) and silicon
Use certified, pathogen-free seeds and avoid prolonged soil water stress
Hot water seed treatment at 53-54°C for 10-12 minutes prior to sowing
management: Maintain appropriate water management to prevent drought stress in the tillering phase
Apply split applications of potash and micronutrient sprays (zinc sulfate)
organic_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum (10 g/kg seed) or Pseudomonas fluorescens
Soil enrichment with farmyard manure (FYM) and vermicompost to improve nutrient holding capacity
Foliar spray with neem oil (3%) or fermented organic concoctions
chemical_management: Mancozeb 75% WP (2 g/L), Propiconazole 25% EC (1 mL/L), or Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP (2 g/L) applied upon early symptom appearance as per local recommendations
diseases.severity_notes: Historically caused the Great Bengal Famine of 1943; severely degrades grain quality, germination percentage, and yield on poor soils.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR-NRRI Guidelines

symptoms: Central vegetative shoot dries up, withers, and turns yellowish-brown ('dead heart')
Affected tiller pulls out easily by hand, revealing chewed base, entry holes, and larval frass
At reproductive stage, identical stem boring leads to erect empty white panicles ('whitehead')
possible_causes: Rice yellow stem borer or striped stem borer moths laying egg masses near leaf tips
Larvae boring inside the stem, severing the vascular bundle and growing tip
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer creating succulent, lush foliage attractive to moths
prevention: Clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting to remove stem borer egg masses
Synchronize planting in the farming block to avoid continuous pest cycles
Avoid excessive nitrogen application; follow balanced split fertilization
Plow fields and submerge stubble immediately after harvest to kill diapausing larvae
management: Install pheromone traps (5-8 traps/ha for monitoring; 20-25 traps/ha for mass trapping)
Conserve natural predators: spiders, dragonflies, and mirid bugs
Rogue and destroy dead heart tillers containing feeding larvae
organic_management: Release Trichogramma japonicum egg parasitoids at 100,000 adults/ha per week starting 30 days after transplanting (total 3-4 releases)
Foliar spray with 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Azadirachtin 1% (2 mL/L)
Install light traps to attract and trap night-flying moths
chemical_management: When pest crosses Economic Threshold Level (ETL: 10% dead hearts or 1 egg mass/m²): Chlorantraniliprole 0.4% G (10 kg/ha), Cartap hydrochloride 4% G (18 kg/ha), or Flubendiamide 39.35% SC (0.25 mL/L) applied per state agricultural university guidance
diseases.severity_notes: Stem borers are key pests of rice; uncontrolled infestations during vegetative stage cause extensive tiller death and yield reductions of 20-70%.
diseases.source: IRRI Pest Knowledge Bank & ICAR-National Research Centre for Integrated Pest Management (NCIPM)

symptoms: Stunted seedlings and plants exhibiting excessive, abnormal tillering ('crazy tiller')
Yellowish-white or pale chlorotic streaks along leaf veins; leaves become thick, twisted, or crinkled
Floral organs proliferate into vegetative leaf-like structures (phyllody) causing malformed, sterile panicles
possible_causes: Soil-borne and water-borne oospores surviving in poorly drained or flooded nursery beds
Prolonged submersion of seedlings during early growth stages in low-lying fields
Infected wild aquatic weed hosts along canals and drainage basins
prevention: Locate nurseries on well-drained, elevated upland seedbeds to avoid stagnant standing water
Avoid using irrigation runoff or floodwater originating from previously infected fields
Rogue and safely destroy severely stunted and malformed tillers
management: Improve drainage channels to prevent prolonged submergence after heavy rains
Eliminate wild grassy weed hosts (e.g. Echinochloa, Digitaria) along bunds and ditches
organic_management: Seed treatment with biocontrol agents (Trichoderma spp.)
Soil incorporation of organic amendments (neem cake) to enhance beneficial microbial soil antagonisms
chemical_management: Seed dressing with Metalaxyl 35% WS (3 g/kg seed) in known endemic nursery locations; foliar spray of Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (2 g/L) if early symptoms appear in seedling beds
diseases.severity_notes: Can result in total sterility of infected hills; sporadic but highly damaging in flood-prone, poorly drained river basin paddies.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Diseases Catalog & Plant Pathology Compendium

symptoms: Adult spiny black beetles scrape leaf chlorophyll, leaving characteristic narrow white parallel streaks
Grubs (larvae) mine between upper and lower leaf epidermises, producing irregular, whitish-translucent blister patches
Severely attacked leaves wither, dry up, and give the entire field an irregular scorched or whitish-bleached appearance
possible_causes: Warm, humid weather following monsoonal showers favoring beetle multiplication
Dense planting and heavy vegetative growth driven by excessive nitrogen fertilizer
Overwintered/summered adult beetles migrating from weed grasses onto young seedlings
prevention: Clip leaf tips of seedlings prior to transplanting to eliminate hispa eggs and leaf-mining larvae
Maintain clean bunds by cutting wild grass hosts before planting
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization and maintain recommended hill spacing for aeration
management: Sweep nursery beds and young crops with fine-mesh hand nets to collect and destroy adult beetles
In deep water paddies, drag a kerosene-soaked rope across the canopy followed by draining to dislodge and destroy beetles
Conserve natural predators including Eulophid parasitoid wasps, spiders, and predatory mirid bugs
organic_management: Foliar spray with 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Azadirachtin 0.03% EC (3 mL/L)
Spraying bio-pesticides such as Beauveria bassiana (1 x 10^8 spores/mL at 5 g/L)
chemical_management: When hispa crosses Economic Threshold Level (ETL: 1-2 adults or 2 damaged leaves per hill): Chlorpyrifos 20% EC (2.5 mL/L), Quinalphos 25% EC (2 mL/L), or Triazophos 40% EC (1.5 mL/L) applied as per local plant protection schedules
diseases.severity_notes: Periodic outbreaks can cause up to 20-50% yield reduction due to extensive loss of photosynthetic leaf area, particularly during tillering.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR-CRRI Integrated Pest Management Bulletins

diseases.scientific_name: Rice Tungro Bacilliform Virus (RTBV) & Rice Tungro Spherical Virus (RTSV)
symptoms: Pronounced plant stunting and significantly reduced tiller count
Leaves turn yellow to bright orange-yellow starting from the tip and moving downward along margins
Young emerging leaves display mottling, light green speckling, and interveinal chlorosis
Delayed flowering with partially exerted, sterile, or small panicles
possible_causes: Dual viral infection by RTBV and RTSV transmitted semi-persistently by the Green Leafhopper (Nephotettix virescens)
Continuous overlapping rice cropping allowing leafhopper vector populations to sustain viral reservoirs
Infected ratoon crops and volunteer rice plants serving as primary infection bridges
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g. IR36, IR64, Vikramarya) possessing tolerance to the viral complex and green leafhopper
Practice synchronized planting across contiguous village farming blocks to break the pest cycle
Plow under rice stubbles and destroy infected volunteer/ratoon plants immediately after harvest
Adopt a crop-free fallow period or rotate with non-host legume/oilseed crops
management: Monitor green leafhopper (GLH) population using yellow sticky traps and light traps
Rogue and safely destroy severely stunted orange-yellow hills during early tillering
Conserve predatory spiders (Lycosa pseudoannulata) and mirid bugs (Cyrtorhinus lividipennis) that feed on GLH
organic_management: Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Neem oil (3%) to repel leafhopper vectors
Apply bio-control agents like Metarhizium anisopliae to suppress leafhopper nymphs
chemical_management: Control insect vector when GLH crosses ETL (1 insect/hill in endemic zones or 2 insects/hill in non-endemic zones): Imidacloprid 17.8% SL (0.3 mL/L), Thiamethoxam 25% WG (0.2 g/L), or Buprofezin 25% SC (1.5 mL/L) targeted to leafhopper feeding zones per extension advice
diseases.severity_notes: One of the most destructive rice virus diseases in South and Southeast Asia; early vegetative infection can cause 70% to 100% crop loss.
diseases.source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank & ICAR-IIRR Tungro Advisory

symptoms: Small, circular to elongate golden-brown to cinnamon-brown powdery pustules (uredinia) on both leaf surfaces
Pustules turn brownish-black late in the season as teleutospores form
Severe foliar infections cause chlorosis, premature leaf senescence, and reduced grain fill
diseases.visual_identification: Powdery rust-colored pustules erupt through the leaf epidermis on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, releasing cinnamon-brown spores when wiped. Differs from Southern Rust (Puccinia polysora), which forms predominantly on the upper leaf surface with smaller, lighter orange pustules.
possible_causes: Airborne fungal urediniospores transported long distances by wind currents
Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C), high relative humidity (>95%), and extended dew periods (6+ hours of leaf wetness)
diseases.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (16-25°C), persistent cloud cover, high relative humidity, and prolonged morning dew.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant or tolerant corn hybrids adapted to the agro-ecological region
Plant early in the season to evade peak spore migration periods
Maintain balanced nitrogen fertilization; avoid excessive nitrogen that promotes overly lush, susceptible foliage
cultural_management: Maintain optimal plant spacing to facilitate airflow within the canopy
Routinely scout lower and middle canopy leaves from vegetative stage V8 through silking
management: Prioritize intervention if pustules appear prior to tasseling/silking on susceptible hybrids under cool, moist weather
biological_management: General preventive guidance (disease-specific biological control is not verified for field eradication of Puccinia sorghi): Rusts are airborne obligate biotrophic fungi. Seed biopriming and soil-applied bioagents do NOT protect against foliar rust.

Preventive foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE; 50 g/L) or certified Bacillus subtilis formulations at earliest pustule sighting provides only mild protective suppression under low disease pressure. (Reference: ICAR-IIMR Technical Bulletin on Maize Diseases & CIMMYT Maize Pathology Manual).
organic_management: General preventive guidance: Preventive spray of 5% neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) at earliest pustule detection offers mild protective suppression. Biological seed treatments do not protect against foliar rust.
chemical_management: Foliar fungicide application is warranted only when rust pustules appear prior to silking on susceptible hybrids under favorable cool, humid weather. The following formulations have official CIB&RC / PPQS label registrations for maize rust: (1) Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Cyproconazole 7.3% SC: 500 mL formulation/ha in 500 L water (1.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 52 days. (2) Kresoxim-methyl 44.3% SC: 500 mL formulation/ha in 500 L water (1.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 25 days. Consult your local agricultural extension officer and use only products registered for this crop and disease in your region. Follow the approved product label.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Pustules can be visually confused with Southern Corn Rust (Puccinia polysora) or early Physoderma brown spot. Accurate diagnosis requires inspecting pustule distribution on both leaf surfaces or microscopic spore examination.
diseases.safety_warnings: Observe mandatory Pre-Harvest Intervals (52 days for Azoxystrobin+Cyproconazole SC; 25 days for Kresoxim-methyl SC). Do not spray after grain reaches the dent stage. Wear protective gear.
diseases.severity_notes: Yield losses range from 10% to 25% if significant leaf blighting occurs prior to or during silking; post-milk infections rarely justify treatment.
diseases.source: PPQS / CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides (Fungicides, ppqs.gov.in) & ICAR-Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR) Technical Bulletins

affected_parts: Lower leaf blades initially, advancing upward to ear leaves and upper canopy
symptoms: Initial pinpoint tan lesions with faint chlorotic haloes on lower leaves
Lesions expand longitudinally between parallel leaf veins into characteristic rectangular, vein-delimited tan to gray necrotic lesions (1-6 cm long)
Lesions turn grayish under high humidity due to conidial sporulation
Extensive lesion coalescence blights entire leaves, causing premature senescence, stalk lodging, and reduced kernel fill
diseases.visual_identification: Strictly vein-bounded, rectangular lesions with blunt, squared-off ends that run parallel to leaf veins. Distinct from Northern Corn Leaf Blight, which produces large elliptical cigar-shaped lesions crossing veins.
possible_causes: Fungal mycelium and conidia surviving in infected corn stover on the soil surface
Warm, humid weather (25-32°C), high relative humidity (>90%), and extended periods of dew or rainfall
diseases.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (25-32°C), high relative humidity (>90%), continuous corn cropping, and heavy morning dews.
prevention: Practice crop rotation with non-cereal host crops (soybeans, pulses) for at least 1-2 seasons
Manage crop residue through clean tillage where conservation practices permit to accelerate stover breakdown
Select corn hybrids with validated genetic resistance or tolerance to Gray Leaf Spot
Avoid high planting densities that restrict canopy airflow and elevate microclimate humidity
cultural_management: Scout lower and middle canopy leaves beginning 2-3 weeks before tasseling
Maintain good field drainage and suppress grass weeds that contribute to canopy humidity
management: Focus management on protecting the ear leaf and leaves above the ear during the critical grain filling window
biological_management: General cultural residue management (disease-specific foliar biological control is not verified for Cercospora zeae-maydis in India): Post-harvest application of Trichoderma inoculants or bio-decomposers onto corn stover accelerates residue breakdown, reducing overwintering fungal survival on the soil surface. (Reference: Ward et al., 1999, Plant Disease, 83(10), pp. 884-895).
Foliar biological sprays provide limited and inconsistent suppression under high disease pressure and are not proven as standalone curative controls.
organic_management: General cultural residue management: Application of Trichoderma inoculants to post-harvest stover helps accelerate crop residue breakdown and reduce fungal overwintering. Foliar bio-agents are not proven standalone controls.
chemical_management: No chemical fungicide has a registered label claim for Gray Leaf Spot on maize under CIB&RC / PPQS in India. Consult your local agricultural extension officer and use only products registered for this crop and disease in your region. Follow the approved product label.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Early pinpoint spots resemble eyespot (Kabatiella zeae) or young Northern Corn Leaf Blight; wait for vein-delimited rectangular expansion before confirming diagnosis.
diseases.safety_warnings: Do not apply unregistered off-label fungicides. Follow regional agricultural extension guidelines and safety protocols.
diseases.severity_notes: One of the most destructive foliar diseases in continuous corn systems; causes significant yield losses and stalk lodging when lesions blight leaves above the ear.
diseases.source: ICAR-IIMR Disease Management Guide & CIMMYT Maize Pathology Manual

affected_parts: Outer ear husks in severe infections
symptoms: Large, elongated, elliptical or cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan necrotic lesions (3-15 cm long)
Lesions have smooth margins with tapered ends, crossing leaf veins without vein limitation
Dark olive-green to black fungal spore mats develop in lesion centers during damp weather
Extensive lesion coalescence causes complete leaf desiccation and burned canopy appearance
diseases.visual_identification: Large cigar-shaped or boat-shaped elliptical lesions with tapered ends that cross parallel veins freely. Unlike Gray Leaf Spot (which is vein-bound and rectangular) and Southern Corn Leaf Blight (which forms smaller, narrower oval lesions).
possible_causes: Fungal conidia surviving in infected maize residue splashed by rain or dispersed by wind onto lower leaves
Moderate temperatures (18-27°C), heavy dews, frequent rain, and prolonged leaf wetness (6-12 hours)
diseases.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18-27°C), heavy morning dews, frequent showers, and 6-12 hours of continuous leaf wetness.
prevention: Cultivate adapted hybrids possessing specific Ht resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, HtN) or polygenic resistance
Implement 1 to 2-year crop rotation away from corn to diminish soil residue inoculum
Ensure balanced potassium and nitrogen nutrition; avoid potassium deficiency which aggravates blight severity
cultural_management: Routinely inspect lower canopy for cigar-shaped lesions from knee-high stage through grain fill
Deeply incorporate crop residue post-harvest where agronomically appropriate
management: Prioritize protection of the ear leaf and upper canopy leaves prior to silking if weather forecasts favor disease progression
biological_management: Seed biopriming: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg seed) helps suppress early seed-borne inoculum and promotes seedling vigor. (Reference: ICAR-IIMR Technical Bulletin, 'Maize Diseases and Their Integrated Management', pp. 18-22).

Foliar protective suppression: Preventive spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE; 50 g/L) at first lesion sighting provides moderate protective suppression under mild disease pressure. (Reference: Harlapur et al., 2007, Karnataka J. Agric. Sci., 20(4), pp. 741-744, URL: http://14.139.155.167/test5/index.php/kjas/article/view/1149).
organic_management: Seed biopriming with Trichoderma viride (10 g/kg seed) to reduce seed-borne infection. Preventive spray of 5% NSKE at initial lesion appearance provides moderate protective suppression.
chemical_management: When 2 to 3 lesions appear on leaves below the ear before silking under humid weather forecasts, apply recommended fungicides. Formulations with specifically verified PPQS label registrations for Turcicum leaf blight on maize: (1) Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Cyproconazole 7.3% SC: 500 mL formulation/ha in 500 L water (1.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 52 days. (2) Kresoxim-methyl 44.3% SC: 500 mL formulation/ha in 500 L water (1.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 25 days. Note on generic registrations: Formulations such as Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC (PHI: 26 days) and Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP (1,000 g/ha in 500 L water; PHI: 37 days) carry PPQS label claims for generic 'maize blight / leaf blight and downy mildew' and are not specifically verified as exclusive Northern Leaf Blight claims. Do not infer that generic 'leaf blight' on product labels specifically verifies efficacy against Northern Leaf Blight. Consult your local agricultural extension officer and use only products registered for this crop and disease in your region. Follow the approved product label.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Provisional Classification & Diagnostic Limitations: The training dataset labeled this class simply as 'Blight'. While visual characteristics (elongated cigar-shaped lesions) and dataset provenance (PlantVillage benchmark) strongly indicate Northern Corn Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum), other maize diseases—including Southern Corn Leaf Blight (Bipolaris maydis), Stewart's bacterial wilt, and physiological leaf firing—can cause overlapping necrotic symptoms. Image-based deep learning predictions provide screening guidance only and must not be treated as definitive laboratory or microscopic confirmation. If severe blight symptoms develop, consult an agricultural extension specialist or plant pathology clinic.
diseases.safety_warnings: Observe mandatory Pre-Harvest Intervals (52 days for Azoxystrobin+Cyproconazole SC; 25 days for Kresoxim-methyl SC; 26 days for Azoxystrobin+Difenoconazole SC; 37 days for Carbendazim+Mancozeb WP). Wear protective equipment.
diseases.severity_notes: Can cause 30-50% grain yield reduction if severe blighting occurs at or before silking; late-season infections after dough stage have minimal yield impact.
diseases.source: PPQS / CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides (Fungicides, ppqs.gov.in) & ICAR-IIMR Maize Pathology Bulletin

symptoms: Uniform vibrant green leaves without chlorotic streaks, necrotic lesions, or pustules
Strong, erect stalk with normal internode spacing and sturdy brace root development
Normal vegetative and reproductive growth appropriate for hybrid phenological stage
diseases.visual_identification: Leaf blades show uniform green pigmentation, intact lamina margins, and absence of fungal pustules, necrotic spots, vascular wilting, or insect-chewed patterns.
diseases.favorable_conditions: Balanced soil fertility, well-drained loamy soil, adequate sunlight, and uniform moisture availability without waterlogging.
prevention: Perform soil test-based balanced NPK fertilization with essential micronutrient (Zinc, Boron) supplementation
Maintain optimal field drainage to prevent waterlogging, particularly during seedling and tasseling stages
Conduct regular weekly scouting for invasive insect pests (e.g. Fall Armyworm) and early foliar spots
Practice integrated weed management during the critical early crop competition window (first 30-45 days)
cultural_management: Continue regular agronomic care, timely irrigation, and split application of nitrogen at knee-high and tasseling stages
management: Maintain optimal plant health through balanced nutrition and routine crop scouting
biological_management: General agronomic fertility guidance (requires local soil-test calibration): Application of well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) or vermicompost (general recommendation: 5-10 t/ha based on local soil test values) during land preparation enriches soil microflora and improves nutrient uptake. This is routine fertility guidance, not disease treatment. (Reference: ICAR-IIMR & CIMMYT Maize Production Manual).
Maintain flowering field borders to conserve beneficial generalist predators (spiders, ladybird beetles, Trichogramma parasitoids) for natural suppression of insect vectors and pests.
organic_management: General agronomic guidance requiring local soil recommendations: Incorporate well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) or vermicompost (5-10 t/ha based on soil test) to foster soil microflora. Conserve natural predators through flowering field borders.
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops. Do not apply synthetic chemical fungicides or prophylactic pesticides to healthy plants.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Visual assessment confirms absence of foliar disease symptoms at the time of inspection. Periodic scouting should continue throughout the growing season as weather conditions change.
diseases.safety_warnings: Avoid unnecessary chemical applications on healthy crops to preserve beneficial insect populations and prevent chemical resistance.
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays healthy vegetative and reproductive growth traits.
diseases.source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR) & CIMMYT Maize Production Manual

diseases.display_name: Early Leaf Spot of Groundnut (Tikka Disease)
symptoms: Subcircular reddish-brown to dark-brown spots (1-10 mm diameter) predominantly on upper leaf surfaces
Distinct, prominent bright yellow chlorotic halo characteristically surrounding each lesion
Severe infection leads to leaflet chlorosis, premature defoliation, and reduced pod yield
diseases.visual_identification: Subcircular reddish-brown spots with prominent bright yellow halos appearing primarily on the upper leaflet surface about 3 to 4 weeks after emergence. Distinct from Late Leaf Spot, which produces darker, nearly black spots on the lower leaf surface with indistinct or absent halos.
possible_causes: Soil-borne conidia and infected groundnut crop residue from previous seasons
Prolonged high relative humidity (>80%), moderate temperatures (25-30°C), and extended leaf wetness from rain or dew
diseases.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (25-30°C), persistent relative humidity (>80%), and frequent rainfall or heavy morning dew.
prevention: Practice 2-year crop rotation with non-legume crops (sorghum, maize, or pearl millet)
Perform deep summer ploughing to bury crop residue and fungal conidia
Sow disease-tolerant or resistant cultivars (e.g., Kadiri-6, Girnar, ICGV series) adapted to the agro-climatic zone
Maintain optimal spacing (30 x 10 cm) to allow canopy aeration and reduce microclimate humidity
cultural_management: Eradicate volunteer groundnut plants and remove infected debris post-harvest
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation late in the evening to prevent prolonged leaf wetness
management: Initiate scouting 3-4 weeks after sowing; apply intervention when spot incidence reaches economic threshold level (5-10% infected leaflets)
biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or Trichoderma harzianum (4-5 g/kg seed) or Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg seed) to suppress early soil-borne inoculum.

Preventive foliar application of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE; 50 g/L) or neem oil (3%) at initial lesion onset offers moderate protective suppression. (Reference: ICAR-DGR Technical Bulletin on Groundnut Diseases).
organic_management: Seed biopriming with Trichoderma viride (4-5 g/kg seed). Foliar application of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) at earliest lesion appearance provides protective suppression under mild disease pressure.
chemical_management: When leaf spots reach economic threshold (5-10% leaflet severity), apply CIB&RC / PPQS registered fungicides: (1) Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP: 1,000 g formulation/ha in 500 L water (2.0 g/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. (2) Tebuconazole 25.9% m/m EC: 500-750 mL/ha in 500 L water (1.0-1.5 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 49 days. (3) Hexaconazole 5% SC: 1,000 mL/ha in 500 L water (2.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. Consult your local agricultural extension officer and follow the approved product label.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Early leaf spot lesions can be confused with early stages of Late Leaf Spot or chemical phytotoxicity burn. Confirmatory identification requires inspecting the yellow halo on the upper surface and microscopic verification of Cercospora conidia.
diseases.safety_warnings: Observe mandatory Pre-Harvest Intervals (30 days for Carbendazim+Mancozeb WP; 49 days for Tebuconazole EC). Wear protective equipment during preparation and spraying. Do not feed treated crop stover to cattle before the PHI has elapsed.
diseases.severity_notes: One of the two major foliar diseases comprising the Groundnut Tikka complex; can cause 15% to 50% pod and haulm yield reduction if left unmanaged.
diseases.source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (ICAR-DGR), Junagadh & CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides (ppqs.gov.in)

diseases.display_name: Late Leaf Spot of Groundnut (Tikka Disease)
diseases.scientific_name: Phaeoisariopsis personata (syn. Cercosporidium personatum / Mycosphaerella berkeleyi)
symptoms: Nearly circular, dark brown to carbonaceous black spots (1-6 mm diameter) appearing primarily on lower leaf surfaces
Lesions typically lack a distinct yellow halo or possess only a very narrow, faint halo
Dense carbonaceous velvety concentric rings of fungal conidiophores visible on the underside of spots
Severe infection leads to rapid extensive defoliation, leaving bare stems with only top leaflets intact
diseases.visual_identification: Dark brown to jet-black spots that are distinctly darker and more pronounced on the abaxial (lower) leaf surface, with rough velvety cushions of conidiophores. Differs from Early Leaf Spot, which is lighter reddish-brown with a prominent bright yellow halo predominantly on the upper leaf surface.
possible_causes: Crop residue, infected seed pods, and wind-borne conidia surviving in soil from previous groundnut cultivation
High relative humidity (>85%), temperatures between 20-26°C, and prolonged leaf wetness (8+ hours)
diseases.favorable_conditions: Cooler to moderate temperatures (20-26°C), persistent cloud cover, relative humidity exceeding 85%, and frequent morning dews.
prevention: Rotate crops with non-host cereals (pearl millet, sorghum, maize) for 2 seasons
Adopt wider row spacing (30-40 cm) to facilitate air circulation and rapid leaf drying
Cultivate tolerant varieties (e.g. Girnar-2, Girnar-3, GPBD-4, ICGV series)
Collect and burn or deeply bury infected haulms post-harvest
cultural_management: Intercrop groundnut with pearl millet or pigeon pea (4:1 or 6:1 ratio) to slow aerial spore dispersal
Avoid water stress during vegetative growth followed by excessive canopy moisture
management: Regularly inspect lower canopy leaves starting 50-60 days after sowing (flowering/pegging stages); treat when 2-3 spots per leaf are observed
biological_management: Seed biopriming with Trichoderma viride or T. harzianum (4-5 g/kg seed) plus Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg seed).

Preventive foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Trichoderma viride formulation (5 g/L) provides partial disease suppression under low-to-moderate disease pressure. (Reference: ICAR-DGR Junagadh & ICRISAT Groundnut Pathology).
organic_management: Seed biopriming with Trichoderma viride (4 g/kg seed). Foliar application of 5% NSKE at initial spot sighting on lower leaves to slow lesion multiplication.
chemical_management: When disease appears on lower leaves at flowering/pegging stages, spray registered fungicides: (1) Tebuconazole 25.9% m/m EC: 500-750 mL/ha in 500 L water (1.0-1.5 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 49 days. (2) Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP: 1,000 g formulation/ha in 500 L water (2.0 g/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. (3) Difenoconazole 25% EC: 500 mL/ha in 500 L water (1.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. Consult local extension authorities and adhere strictly to label guidelines.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Late leaf spot frequently co-occurs with groundnut rust in the field, forming a destructive disease complex. Lesions must be distinguished from early leaf spot by checking lower surface cushion texture and darker coloration.
diseases.safety_warnings: Adhere strictly to Pre-Harvest Intervals (49 days for Tebuconazole EC; 30 days for Carbendazim+Mancozeb WP). Avoid spraying during windy conditions or before rain. Wear protective mask and gloves.
diseases.severity_notes: Generally more destructive than Early Leaf Spot; severe defoliation during pod development can result in yield losses up to 50-70% and severely degrades haulm fodder quality.
diseases.source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (ICAR-DGR), Junagadh & CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides (ppqs.gov.in)

symptoms: Small, circular, raised blisters or pustules (uredinia) measuring 0.5-1.5 mm on the lower leaf surface
Pustules rupture the epidermis to expose bright orange to cinnamon-brown powdery mass of urediniospores
Corresponding upper leaf surface shows pale yellow chlorotic flecks directly above the pustules
Infected leaves curl upward, turn necrotic, dry out, and appear burned while remaining attached to the plant (no premature defoliation, unlike Tikka leaf spots)
diseases.visual_identification: Raised circular blisters on lower leaf surfaces discharging reddish-brown powdery spores when rubbed with a finger. Unlike Early and Late Leaf Spots which cause extensive leaf dropping, rust-infected leaves dry up, curl, and remain attached to the stem.
possible_causes: Airborne fungal urediniospores carried over long distances by wind currents
Moderate temperatures (20-25°C), high relative humidity (>85%), and extended periods of free water on leaf surfaces
diseases.favorable_conditions: Temperatures between 20-25°C, relative humidity above 85%, frequent light showers or heavy night dews, and dense planting.
prevention: Sow rust-resistant/tolerant cultivars (e.g., GPBD-4, ICGV-91114, Girnar-1, ALR-3)
Avoid staggered sowings in neighboring fields to prevent continuous disease cycle
Intercrop groundnut with non-host cereals (pearl millet, sorghum, maize)
Eradicate self-sown groundnut plants between crop seasons
cultural_management: Maintain adequate plant spacing to facilitate airflow within the canopy
Avoid excess nitrogen application that produces dense, succulent foliage
management: Scout crops weekly from 40 days after sowing; initiate preventive measures when the first pustules appear on lower leaves
biological_management: Foliar spray of fungal hyperparasites such as Acremonium persicinum or Verticillium lecanii (1 x 10^8 spores/mL) has demonstrated biocontrol potential in research trials against Puccinia arachidis.

Preventive spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE; 50 g/L) or Neem oil (3%) inhibits urediniospore germination and provides mild protective suppression under low disease pressure. (Reference: ICAR-DGR Technical Bulletin on Groundnut Rust).
organic_management: Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or 3% neem oil upon observing initial pustules. Plant resistant cultivars such as GPBD-4.
chemical_management: Apply registered fungicides when pustules appear on lower leaves: (1) Hexaconazole 5% SC: 1,000 mL/ha in 500 L water (2.0 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. (2) Tebuconazole 25.9% m/m EC: 500-750 mL/ha in 500 L water (1.0-1.5 mL/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 49 days. (3) Mancozeb 75% WP: 1,000-1,250 g/ha in 500 L water (2.0-2.5 g/L); Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): 30 days. Consult local extension authorities and adhere strictly to label guidelines.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Early rust flecks can resemble early leaf spots or mite feeding stipples before pustules erupt. Rubbing the spot with a white tissue to check for orange-brown spore residue confirms active sporulation.
diseases.safety_warnings: Observe mandatory Pre-Harvest Intervals (30 days for Hexaconazole SC and Mancozeb WP; 49 days for Tebuconazole EC). Wear protective equipment during application.
diseases.severity_notes: Can cause up to 50% pod yield reduction and severely damages fodder quality when combined with Late Leaf Spot; early vegetative rust infection causes severe economic losses.
diseases.source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (ICAR-DGR), Junagadh & CIB&RC Major Uses of Pesticides (ppqs.gov.in)

symptoms: Iron Chlorosis: Vivid interveinal yellowing of young apical leaflets while main veins remain sharply green; in severe cases, entire leaflets turn pale ivory-white
Zinc Deficiency: Stunted plant growth, small crinkled leaflets ('little leaf' appearance), and chlorotic mottling between veins
Nitrogen Deficiency: Uniform pale green to light yellow discoloration of older basal leaves progressing upward throughout the canopy with reduced nodulation
Complete absence of fungal pustules, necrotic spots with yellow halos, or pathogenic fruiting bodies
diseases.visual_identification: Patterned chlorosis (interveinal yellowing or generalized leaf yellowing) without discrete necrotic spots, fungal pustules, concentric rings, or spore mats. Tissues remain supple and intact without fungal sporulation.
possible_causes: High soil pH / calcareous soils (>7.5 pH) immobilizing iron and zinc in insoluble carbonate forms
Imbalanced fertilizer application, low soil organic matter, or poor soil drainage causing temporary root hypoxia
diseases.favorable_conditions: Calcareous black clay soils, high bicarbonate levels in irrigation water, prolonged saturated soil conditions, and low organic carbon.
prevention: Perform soil testing prior to sowing to determine exact micronutrient and macronutrient status
Apply well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM; 10-12 t/ha) or vermicompost to improve soil organic carbon and nutrient chelation
Apply Gypsum (400-500 kg/ha) in two splits: 50% at sowing and 50% at flowering/pegging (40-45 DAS) for calcium and sulfur supply
Inoculate seed with Rhizobium and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) biofertilizers
cultural_management: Avoid over-irrigation and waterlogging in heavy soils which precipitates iron chlorosis
Ensure proper field drainage and intercultural hoeing to aerate the root zone
management: Identify specific deficiency pattern (interveinal vs general) and apply targeted foliar micronutrient correction promptly
biological_management: Biofertilizer seed inoculation: Seed treatment with Bradyrhizobium groundnut culture (200-250 g/10 kg seed) and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB; 200 g/10 kg seed) enhances biological nitrogen fixation and phosphorus uptake.
Incorporate bio-enriched compost with mycorrhizal fungi (VAM) to improve root absorption of zinc, iron, and phosphorus.
organic_management: Apply well-decomposed FYM (10-12 t/ha) enriched with Trichoderma and Pseudomonas. Use Rhizobium and PSB seed treatment. Incorporate green manure crops (sunnhemp or sesbania) before sowing.
chemical_management: This is a non-infectious physiological condition; DO NOT apply synthetic fungicides. Apply targeted nutrient sprays: (1) Iron Chlorosis: Foliar spray of Ferrous Sulphate (FeSO4, 0.5% = 5 g/L) + Citric acid (0.1% = 1 g/L) at 30 and 45 days after sowing (2-3 sprays at 7-10 day intervals). (2) Zinc Deficiency: Foliar spray of Zinc Sulphate (ZnSO4, 0.5% = 5 g/L) or soil application of Zinc Sulphate (25 kg/ha at sowing). (3) General Chlorosis: Foliar spray of 19:19:19 water-soluble NPK (1.0% = 10 g/L).
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Interveinal chlorosis caused by iron deficiency can be confused with Groundnut Bud Necrosis Virus (GBNV) chlorotic ring mottling or early spider mite infestation. Absence of concentric ring necrosis and lack of insect webbing confirms nutritional etiology.
diseases.safety_warnings: Always neutralize ferrous sulphate spray solution with citric acid to prevent iron precipitation. Do not apply fertilizer sprays during hot midday hours to prevent foliar salt burn; spray early morning or late afternoon.
diseases.severity_notes: Severe iron chlorosis in calcareous soils can reduce pod yield by 20% to 40% and severely impairs root nodulation; timely foliar correction restores vegetative vigor within 7-10 days.
diseases.source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (ICAR-DGR), Junagadh & TNAU Agronomy Groundnut Portal

symptoms: Uniform vibrant green tetrafoliate leaves with intact leaflets and smooth margins
Sturdy erect or spreading stems with healthy flowering nodes and normal peg penetration
Complete absence of fungal spots, rust pustules, chlorotic streaks, or deficiency yellowing
diseases.visual_identification: Leaflets exhibit uniform deep green coloration, firm turgid texture, and clean upper and lower surfaces free from pustules, necrotic spots, chlorotic halos, or chewing damage.
diseases.favorable_conditions: Well-drained sandy loam to loamy soil (pH 6.0-7.5), optimal daytime temperatures (25-30°C), adequate soil moisture during pegging, and full sunlight.
prevention: Maintain balanced soil fertility (NPK: 20-40-40 kg/ha or soil test recommendation)
Apply gypsum (400-500 kg/ha) at flowering/pegging for pod filling and shell hardness
Perform regular weekly scouting for foliar spots, leaf miners, and sucking pests
Ensure optimal field drainage to prevent water stagnation
cultural_management: Continue routine agronomic care, timely weeding up to 35-40 DAS (avoid hoeing after pegging), and critical-stage irrigations (flowering, pegging, pod development)
management: Maintain optimum crop health through balanced nutrition, timely irrigations, and routine IPM monitoring
biological_management: Maintain soil biological health by applying well-composted farmyard manure (FYM; 7.5-10 t/ha) during final land preparation.
Conserve natural biological control agents (ladybird beetles, spiders, predatory mites) by avoiding prophylactic chemical pesticide sprays on healthy crops.
organic_management: Apply compost or vermicompost (2.5 t/ha). Inoculate seeds with Rhizobium and PSB biofertilizers. Avoid unwarranted chemical applications to preserve soil microbiome and beneficial insects.
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops. Do NOT apply prophylactic synthetic chemical fungicides or pesticides to healthy foliage.
diseases.diagnostic_limitations: Visual health indicates absence of foliar disease symptoms at the time of observation. Continue weekly monitoring, especially during flowering and pod development as weather changes.
diseases.safety_warnings: Avoid unwarranted chemical applications on healthy plants to preserve beneficial soil and canopy biodiversity and prevent pesticide resistance.
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays normal healthy vegetative and reproductive growth characteristics.
diseases.source: ICAR-Directorate of Groundnut Research (ICAR-DGR), Junagadh & ICRISAT Groundnut Production Guidelines

symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown to black with yellow halo
Spots coalesce causing extensive leaf blighting, premature defoliation, and fruit lesions with blister-like scabs
Severe defoliation exposes fruit to sunscald and drastically reduces yield
possible_causes: Seed-borne bacterium or infected crop debris in soil
Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with persistent high humidity and driving rain / overhead splashing
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 seasons
Adopt drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to prevent water splash transmission
management: At earliest symptom appearance, apply protective copper sprays and remove heavily infected lower foliage
organic_management: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed
Foliar spray of 1% Bordeaux mixture or copper hydroxide early in the morning
Spray fresh fermented buttermilk (10%) or 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) as bio-protective barrier
chemical_management: Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L + Streptocycline (Streptomycin sulphate + Tetracycline) @ 100 mg/L (1 g in 10 L water)
Copper Hydroxide 77% WP @ 2.0 g/L at 10-14 day intervals during rainy spells; observe 15-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Bacterial spot can cause up to 50-60% defoliation and severe fruit drop if left uncontrolled during wet monsoon periods.
diseases.source: ANGRAU Chilli Advisory / ICAR-IIVR Varanasi / TNAU Agritech Portal

diseases.display_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot of Chilli (Frogeye Spot)
symptoms: Circular lesions with ash-grey or white centers surrounded by distinct dark-brown or reddish margins ('frogeye' appearance)
Lesions may enlarge up to 1 cm, become papery, and drop out leaving a 'shot-hole' effect
Severely infected leaves turn chlorotic, senesce prematurely, and drop
possible_causes: Air-borne conidia and resting fungal mycelium on crop residue
High humidity (>80%) and temperatures between 20-28°C with frequent cloud cover
prevention: Deep summer ploughing to bury fungal conidia and previous harvest residue
Maintain 60 x 45 cm spacing to provide adequate canopy aeration
Grow tolerant cultivars (e.g. LCA 334, G-4, Aparna) recommended for the zone
management: Begin scouting from 30 days after transplanting; initiate protective fungicidal spray at initial spot detection
organic_management: Foliar spray of Trichoderma viride or T. harzianum @ 5 g/L with cow milk (1%) as spreader
Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or 3% Neem oil at 10-day intervals
Application of Jeevamrit (10%) to promote foliar antagonistic microflora
chemical_management: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as protective spray
Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L for curative control; observe 14-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Cercospora leaf spot causes extensive premature defoliation in Krishna-Godavari basin chilli belts, reducing photosynthesis and pod size.
diseases.source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR) / ANGRAU Lam Farm Guntur

symptoms: Upward leaf curling, puckering, crinkling, and reduction in leaf lamina size
Thickened veins, shortened internodes causing severe plant stunting and bushy 'witches broom' appearance
Flower abortion and deformed, small, wrinkled pods resulting in drastic crop loss
possible_causes: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) vectors transmitting the begomovirus from alternate weeds or solanaceous hosts
Hot, dry spells during early vegetative growth favoring vector multiplication
prevention: Erect yellow sticky cards (15-20 per acre) and blue sticky cards to monitor and trap vector insects
Grow 2-3 barrier rows of maize, sorghum, or bajra around the chilli field to impede whitefly flight
Eradicate alternate host weeds (Parthenium, Datura, Abutilon) along field bunds
management: Rogue out and destroy viral-infected plants during early vegetative phase before vector transmission spreads
organic_management: Nursery protection using 40-mesh insect-proof nylon net
Foliar spray of cold-pressed Neem oil (10,000 ppm) @ 3.0 ml/L + liquid detergent (0.5 ml/L)
Release of bio-predator Chrysoperla carnea @ 10,000 larvae/acre to consume whitefly nymphs
chemical_management: Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.2 g/L targeting adult whiteflies
Pyriproxyfen 10% EC @ 2.0 ml/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1.0 ml/L to inhibit whitefly nymph growth; observe 15-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Chilli leaf curl virus is the most destructive viral disease in South Indian chilli cultivation; can cause 70-100% economic yield loss if infection occurs before flowering.
diseases.source: ICAR-Central Institute for Arid Horticulture / ANGRAU Chilli Pathology Advisory 2024

symptoms: Uniform green, smooth leaf lamina without curling, spots, chlorosis, or necrotic margins
Normal branching, robust internode elongation, and balanced flowering
Intact apical buds and healthy white root system
prevention: Balanced soil application of NPK (150:60:150 kg/ha) with split nitrogen fertigation
Regular preventive scouting for sucking pests and foliar spots every 5 days
management: Continue scheduled irrigation and weed-free bund management
organic_management: Monthly soil drenching with Jeevamrit and foliar application of Panchagavya (3%)
chemical_management: No chemical fungicides or insecticides required
diseases.severity_notes: Healthy plant exhibiting optimal vegetative and reproductive development.
diseases.source: ICAR-IIVR / ANGRAU Package of Practices for Chilli

diseases.scientific_name: Physiological Nutrient Disorder (N-P-K / Fe / Zn / Mg)
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between green leaf veins) on young or older leaves
Nitrogen deficiency causes generalized pale yellowing starting from bottom leaves upward
Iron or zinc deficiency causes prominent interveinal ivory/yellow whitening on terminal growing flushes
Absence of fungal sporulation, bacterial water-soaking, or insect vectors
possible_causes: Alkaline or saline soil pH (>7.8) locking up micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese)
Waterlogged or highly compacted soil reducing nutrient uptake
Imbalanced fertilizer application without micronutrient supplementation
prevention: Apply balanced basal fertilizer along with well-decomposed Farm Yard Manure (FYM @ 10 t/acre)
Conduct soil and leaf petiole test before transplanting to determine precise nutrient dosages
management: Apply targeted foliar micronutrient correction sprays during vegetative and flowering stages
organic_management: Apply enriched compost or vermicompost (2 tonnes/acre) mixed with biofertilizers (Azospirillum, PSB @ 2 kg/acre)
Foliar spray of seaweed extract (2 ml/L) or humic acid (3 ml/L) to enhance nutrient absorption
chemical_management: For general micronutrient deficiency: Foliar spray of Grade-IV / Formula-4 Micronutrient mixture @ 2.5 g/L
For Zinc deficiency: Zinc sulphate (ZnSO4 21%) @ 2.0 g/L + citric acid (0.5 g/L)
For Iron deficiency: Ferrous sulphate (FeSO4 19%) @ 3.0 g/L + citric acid (0.5 g/L) at 10-day intervals
diseases.severity_notes: Nutrient deficiencies weaken plant defense mechanisms, reduce flowering by 30-40%, and predispose plants to secondary fungal infections.
diseases.source: ICAR-Indian Institute of Spices Research (IISR) / ANGRAU Micronutrient Bulletin

diseases.display_name: White Spot / Powdery Mildew of Chilli
symptoms: White to grayish powdery fungal growth on the lower leaf surface with corresponding chlorotic yellow patches on the upper surface
In severe stages, fungal lesions turn into prominent bleached white-gray spots with necrotic centers
Leaves curl downward, wither, and drop prematurely, leaving bare branches with exposed pods
possible_causes: Warm daytime temperatures (25-32°C) combined with high relative humidity and dry winds
Dense plant canopy with restricted sunlight and stagnant air
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen application which promotes soft, succulent foliar growth
Provide adequate plant spacing (60 x 45 cm) and orient rows in prevailing wind direction
Clean bunds and remove wild solanaceous host weeds
management: Scout lower canopy leaves regularly during flowering and fruit development; spray at earliest sign of white mycelium
organic_management: Foliar spray of wettable sulphur 80% WDG @ 2.5 g/L early in the morning before sun heat
Foliar spray of 10% sour fermented buttermilk or 0.5% baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) solution
Spray Ampelomyces quisqualis (bio-fungicide) @ 5 g/L against powdery mildew mycelium
chemical_management: Sulfur 80% WDG @ 3.0 g/L water or Dinocap 48% EC @ 1.0 ml/L at initial symptom appearance
Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 1.5 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Penconazole 10% EC @ 0.5 ml/L; observe 14-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Powdery mildew and white spot can cause up to 40% leaf loss and severe sunscald on chilli pods in semi-arid and sub-humid zones.
diseases.source: ANGRAU Chilli Protection Manual / ICAR-IIVR Varanasi Technical Bulletin

symptoms: Large oval or diamond-shaped pale brown lesions with prominent bright yellow halo borders
Lesions typically start along the leaf margins and expand inward with faint concentric zonations
Under humid conditions, grayish-brown velvety fungal sporulation develops on the underside of necrotic spots
possible_causes: Prolonged leaf wetness and warm temperatures (24-30°C)
Poor field drainage and dense unpruned plantation canopies
prevention: Maintain optimal plant spacing (1.8 x 1.8 m or 2.1 x 2.1 m) to improve canopy aeration
Regular desuckering and removal of dead hanging leaves to reduce humidity
Ensure proper surface and sub-surface soil drainage during monsoon seasons
management: Prune and safely burn or bury heavily spotted lower leaves before fungal sporulation
Apply foliar protective sprays during early monsoon or initial symptom detection
organic_management: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L with sticker
Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/L or Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L
Neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or 1% horticultural mineral oil spray
chemical_management: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at early lesion appearance
Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L; observe 21-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Cordana leaf spot causes significant functional photosynthetic area loss in banana plantations during rainy seasons, leading to smaller bunch sizes.
diseases.source: ICAR-NRCB National Research Centre for Banana / FAO Banana Compendium

symptoms: Broad, erect, glossy emerald green leaves without necrotic lesions or chlorosis
Sturdy pseudostem with clean sheath overlap and vigorous continuous bunch emergence
Well-anchored root system with active white feeder rootlets
prevention: Balanced fertigation scheduling (N-P-K based on tissue and soil testing)
Regular desuckering keeping only one mother plant and one selected follower ratoon
Mulching around pseudostem base to conserve moisture and regulate root temperature
management: Continue standard agronomic practices, weed management, and periodic pest monitoring
organic_management: Apply well-decomposed FYM (20 kg/plant) or vermicompost (5 kg/plant) with biofertilizers (Azospirillum, PSB)
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays vigorous healthy vegetative growth.
diseases.source: ICAR-NRCB Banana Package of Practices

symptoms: Small yellowish or reddish-brown circular spots expanding into irregular bleached grayish-white lesions
Dark brown to black raised margin separating diseased necrotic tissue from green blade
Tiny black punctiform pustules (acervuli) visible under hand lens on the bleached central zone
possible_causes: Opportunistic fungal colonization following wind damage, mechanical bruising, or insect punctures
Persistent high relative humidity (>85%) and temperature between 22°C and 28°C
prevention: Erect windbreaks around banana plantations to prevent wind tear and mechanical leaf tearing
Avoid damaging foliage during weeding and de-suckering operations
Maintain soil potassium levels to strengthen epidermal leaf cell walls
management: Sanitize canopy by cutting off dried necrotic leaf tips and diseased leaves
Ensure rapid canopy drying by pruning unproductive side suckers
organic_management: Copper Hydroxide 77% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Bordeaux mixture 1% spray
Foliar spray of Bacillus subtilis biocontrol formulations @ 5 g/L
chemical_management: Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L for advancing infections
diseases.severity_notes: Pestalotiopsis weakens functional leaf surface and accelerates premature senescence, especially when combined with wind damage.
diseases.source: ICAR-NRCB Tiruchirappalli Technical Manual / CABI Crop Protection

symptoms: Small faint yellowish-green specks parallel to leaf veins developing into reddish-brown to black spindle streaks
Centers of older lesions become sunken, bleached ash-grey with prominent dark brown margins and bright yellow halos
Extensive coalescence of spots leads to rapid leaf blighting, premature leaf collapse, and unfilled bunches
possible_causes: Warm humid tropical weather with frequent rainfall or heavy dew (>90% RH, 25-30°C)
Stagnant microclimate in densely planted stands with poor air circulation
prevention: Adhere to recommended wider spacing (2.1 x 2.1 m) to maximize wind passage
Systematic de-leafing: remove and bury severely infected leaves at weekly intervals during rainy periods
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; prefer drip systems to keep foliar canopy dry
management: Implement early-season fungicide rotations targeting younger emerging leaves (first 3-4 leaves)
organic_management: Spray horticultural mineral oil (1% emulsion) combined with Copper Oxychloride @ 2.0 g/L
Bio-fungicide foliar applications of Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/L + cow urine 5%
chemical_management: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L mixed with 1% mineral oil
Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Trifloxystrobin 25% + Tebuconazole 50% WG @ 0.7 g/L; rotate chemical classes to prevent resistance
diseases.severity_notes: Sigatoka is the most economically devastating foliar disease of banana worldwide, causing up to 50% yield reduction and premature ripening of bunches during transit.
diseases.source: CIMMYT / ICAR-NRCB Banana Pathology Guidelines

symptoms: Uniform vibrant green upright leaf blades without chlorosis, pustules, or blotches
Vigorous tillering and healthy crown root development
Uniform spike emergence and clean glumes
prevention: Sow certified disease-free seeds treated with Trichoderma or standard seed protectant
Balanced fertilizer application (120:60:40 kg NPK/ha based on soil test)
Timely irrigation at critical growth stages (crown root initiation, tillering, jointing, flowering, milk stage)
management: Continue standard wheat field management, weed control, and periodic rust scouting
organic_management: Application of well-cured compost (10 t/ha), Azotobacter and PSB seed treatment
chemical_management: None required for healthy crops
diseases.severity_notes: Not applicable - plant displays healthy vegetative growth.
diseases.source: ICAR-IIWBR Karnal Wheat Package of Practices

symptoms: Small, circular to oval orange-brown or reddish-brown powdery pustules (uredinia) scattered randomly over the upper leaf surface
Pustules rupture the upper leaf epidermis, shedding millions of fine rust-colored spores upon contact
Severely rusted leaves turn yellow, chlorotic, and wither prematurely, shriveling grain fill
possible_causes: Moderate temperatures (15-25°C) coupled with overnight dew formation and free moisture on leaf blades
Airborne transport of urediniospores from warm winter-growing regions
prevention: Cultivate certified rust-resistant wheat varieties (e.g., HD-2967, DBW-187, DBW-303, PBW-725)
Avoid late sowing to prevent exposure to warm late-spring rust buildup
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which creates succulent foliage highly susceptible to rust colonization
management: Regular weekly scouting of flag leaves during booting and flowering; initiate action at first pustule appearance
organic_management: Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or bio-fungicide Bacillus amyloliquefaciens @ 5 g/L
Foliar spray of cow urine (10%) mixed with fermented butter milk
chemical_management: Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L (500 ml/ha in 500 L water) at the very first sign of brown pustules
Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L; observe 30-day PHI
diseases.severity_notes: Leaf rust can reduce wheat yield by 20% to 50% and severely decrease thousand-kernel weight (TKW) when flag leaves are infected before grain filling.
diseases.source: ICAR-IIWBR Indian Institute of Wheat & Barley Research / CIMMYT Wheat Pathology

symptoms: Generalized uniform pale green to pale yellow discoloration (chlorosis) initiating on the oldest lower leaves
Yellowing begins at the leaf tip and progresses down the midrib toward the leaf base in a distinct 'V' shape
Stunted erect plant growth, reduced tiller numbers, thin stems, and small pale spikes
possible_causes: Insufficient nitrogen fertilizer application or severe leaching in sandy soils due to excessive irrigation or heavy rains
Waterlogged soil conditions inducing denitrification and inhibiting root nitrogen absorption
prevention: Conduct pre-sowing soil fertility tests to calculate nitrogen deficit
Split application of nitrogen: 50% basal dose at sowing, 25% at first irrigation (CRI stage), and 25% at second irrigation (tillering/jointing)
Incorporate green manure crops (Sesbania) or farmyard manure prior to field preparation
management: Apply immediate nitrogen top-dressing before irrigating the crop
For rapid leaf absorption, administer foliar urea sprays
organic_management: Foliar application of liquid Jeevamrut @ 10% or vermiwash @ 5% during vegetative stages
Seed inoculation with Azotobacter biofertilizer (200 g/10 kg seed)
chemical_management: Top-dressing with Prilled Urea @ 25-35 kg/acre just prior to irrigation
Foliar spray of 2.0% Urea solution (20 g Urea/L water) for rapid recovery under standing crop conditions
diseases.severity_notes: Nitrogen deficiency directly curtails tillering capacity and grain protein content, leading to drastic yield reductions (up to 40%).
diseases.source: ICAR-IIWBR Nutrient Management Guidelines / FAO Fertilizer Manual
